key_findings: The skill provides a consistent report template (Summary table, Issues/Improvements separation) that baseline lacks — this is the main structural benefit
Baseline failed 1 assertion in Eval 1: Issues and Improvements were not separated into distinct sections
For Eval 2 (i18n) and Eval 3 (security/perf), both approaches passed all assertions equally
Baseline was slightly faster on average (190.9s vs 199.7s) but used more tokens (63.4K vs 60.9K)
The skill-guided reports are shorter and more focused; baseline reports tend to be more exploratory and include extra sections (Accessibility Review, Positive Patterns)
non_discriminating_assertions: has-file-refs — both approaches consistently reference specific files with line numbers
has-code-examples — both include multiple code examples
covers-all-files — both review all specified files
no-false-positives — both self-correct when a finding is incorrect
checks-both-locales — both examine both locale files
xss-check — both thoroughly examine XSS vectors
discriminating_assertions: has-structure — skill enforces Summary table + Issues/Improvements separation; baseline merges them
qualitative_observations: The with-skill reports follow the template format consistently, making them easier to parse programmatically and convert to Beads tasks
The without-skill reports are more creative — they add Accessibility Review, Positive Patterns, structural observations that the skill template doesn't call for
Both approaches find similar core issues (stale closures, React.memo defeated, i18n pluralization bugs)
The baseline sometimes finds MORE issues because it explores more freely (16 findings vs 14 in Eval 1)
